query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Hot forging near 900 °C followed by a short annealing step at ~800 °C will refine the dual-phase lamellar microstructure, disperse dislocation pile-ups, and reduce stress concentrations at internal boundaries, thereby increasing room-temperature ductility by at least 20% and maintaining or slightly improving yield strength relative to the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing involving hot forging at ~900 °C and short annealing at ~800 °C to reduce lamellar spacing and refine boundary structures.
generation.conditions: Post-processing room-temperature tensile tests at ~10^-3 s^-1 strain rate. Operating environment adheres to typical laboratory conditions without special atmospheric constraints.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar boundaries and reduced interlamellar spacing in the dual-phase microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The refined lamellar microstructure disperses dislocation pile-ups by shortening the mean free path and reducing the local stress concentrations at interfaces, lowering the driving force for microcrack nucleation and delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: At least a 20% increase in ductility compared to the as-cast condition, with yield strength maintained or slightly improved.
generation.baseline: Untreated (as-cast) eutectic high-entropy alloy with coarse lamellae that exhibits early dislocation pile-up, microcracking, and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: If forging or annealing are conducted at temperatures or durations that coarsen the lamellae or alter phase fractions severely, the beneficial effects on ductility and strength are reduced or lost.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement depends on precise forging parameters (time, temperature, strain rate) and alloy chemistry; excessive or insufficient deformation may complicate the final microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare test coupons from the as-cast alloy, then subject them to forging at ~900 °C and anneal at ~800 °C for a short duration. Perform uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature to compare mechanical behavior against untreated control samples.
measurements: Tensile elongation and yield strength at 10^-3 s^-1 strain rate
Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) of lamellar spacing and dislocation substructures
Evaluation of microcrack initiation sites near interfaces by postmortem fractography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-treatment samples do not exhibit at least a 20% increase in ductility or do not maintain/improve yield strength compared to the as-cast reference, or if early microcracks persist at lamellar boundaries under identical testing conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. AbstractMulti-principal element alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are emerging metallic materials with unprecedented structures and properties for various applications. In this study, we tuned the microstructure and mechanical performance of a recently designed high-performance Co-rich TRIP-HEA via thermomechanical processing (TMP). The microstructures of the HEA after various TMP routines were characterized, and their correlation with room-temperature tensile performance was clarified. The results showed that grain refinement is an effective strategy for enhancing strength while retaining satisfactory ductility. The formation of incoherent precipitates slightly improves the strength but inevitably sacrifices the ductility, which needs to be considered for optimizing the TMPs. The room temperature tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength were increased from 254.6 to 641.3 MPa and from 702.5 to 968.4 MPa, respectively, but the tensile elongation retains a satisfactory value of 68.8%. chosen.technique: hot forging plus short anneal to refine lamellar microstructure
chosen.conditions: uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (e.g., 10^-3 s^-1 strain rate) following forging near 900°C and short annealing at ~800°C
chosen.why: By reducing lamellar spacing and controlling boundary structure through thermomechanical processing, dislocation pile-ups are dispersed, mitigating local stress concentrations and microcracking. Prior studies on high-entropy alloys and advanced steels show that microstructural refinement improves both ductility and strength. We predict at least a 20% increase in tensile ductility compared to the as-cast state, along with maintained or slightly improved yield strength. A falsification experiment would examine whether microcracks persist via in situ or postmortem microscopy under tensile load. If microcracks remain dominant, causing early failure, the hypothesis is invalidated.
